## Hard

### 2H1
\

<details>

<summary>Click to show answer</summary>

We have two hypotheses:

- $A$: The panda belongs to species A.
- $B$: The panda belongs to species B.

The problem gives us the following information:

|  | Species A | Species B |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Prior probability | 0.50 | 0.50 |
| Probability of twins | 0.10 | 0.20 |
| Probability of singleton | 0.90 | 0.80 |

We will use $T$ for a twin birth, $S$ for a single birth. We will also make explicit the assumption that the birth outcomes are independent conditional on the mother's species (that is, once we know the mother's species then there is no other information available that could be used to change the probability of the outcome of a future birth).

We know the mother has already given birth to twins. We want:

$$
P(T_2\mid T_1)
$$

where $T_1$ represents twins on the first birth and $T_2$ twins on the second.

Note that **the first twin birth changes our beliefs about the mother's species**.

Before observing the first birth, we had:

$$
P(A)=P(B)=0.5
$$

After observing twins, we apply Bayes' theorem:

$$
P(A\mid T_1)
=\frac{P(T_1\mid A)P(A)}{P(T_1)}
$$

The denominator is calculated using the law of total probability:

$$
P(T_1)=P(T_1\mid A)P(A)+P(T_1\mid B)P(B)
$$

Substituting:

$$
P(T_1)=(0.1)(0.5)+(0.2)(0.5)=0.15
$$

Therefore:

$$
P(A\mid T_1)=\frac{0.1(0.5)}{0.15}=\frac13
$$

Similarly:

$$
P(B\mid T_1)=\frac23
$$

We now have updated beliefs about the species. The second birth can be twins under either hypothesis, so:

$$
P(T_2\mid T_1)
=P(T_2\mid A)P(A\mid T_1)+P(T_2\mid B)P(B\mid T_1)
$$

Substituting:

$$
=\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)\left(\frac13\right)
+\left(\frac15\right)\left(\frac23\right)
$$

$$
P(T_2\mid T_1)=\frac16\approx16.67\%
$$


The probability we calculated is greater than the original probability of 15%. Since observing twins makes species B more plausible, and species B has a higher twin-birth rate, we would expect some increase in our resulting probability.

</details>

### 2H2
\

<details>

<summary>Click to show answer</summary>

This is actually the intermediate calculated we performed in the earlier question.

Using our notation from part 1: 

We want:

$$
P(A\mid T)
$$

Using Bayes' theorem:

$$
P(A\mid T)=
\frac{P(T\mid A)P(A)}
{P(T\mid A)P(A)+P(T\mid B)P(B)}
$$

$$
=\frac{(0.1)(0.5)}
{(0.1)(0.5)+(0.2)(0.5)}
$$

$$
P(A\mid T)=\frac13\approx33.33\%
$$

We were originally given $P(T|A)$ which is a description of how likely the observation of twins is under our hypothesis that the panda is species A. What we just calculated is how plausible our hypothesis of species A is given that we have observed the event that twins were born. 

</details>

### 2H3
\

<details>

<summary>Click to show answer</summary>

Now we have a second birth, this time a single.

We now want:

$$
P(A\mid T_1,S_2)
$$

From the second part, our updated probabilities are:

$$
P(A\mid T_1)=\frac13,\qquad P(B\mid T_1)=\frac23
$$

We can treat these as the priors for our next update.

$$
P(A\mid T_1,S_2)=
\frac{P(S_2\mid A)P(A\mid T_1)}
{P(S_2\mid A)P(A\mid T_1)+P(S_2\mid B)P(B\mid T_1)}
$$

Substituting:

$$
=\frac{0.9(\frac13)}
{0.9(\frac13)+0.8(\frac23)}
$$

$$
=\frac{0.3}{0.3+0.53333}
$$

$$
P(A\mid T_1,S_2)=0.36
$$

This problem is a useful demonstration of sequential Bayesian inference. Note that the evidence does not necessarily push us **consistently** toward one hypothesis, we now consider species A to be slightly more plausible. 

</details>



### 2H4
\

<details>

<summary>Click to show answer</summary>

We now have an updated collection of information.

|  | Species A | Species B |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Prior probability | 0.50 | 0.50 |
| Probability of twins | 0.10 | 0.20 |
| Probability of singleton | 0.90 | 0.80 |
| Probability test says A | 0.80 | 0.35 |

With our new addition, we will use $+$ for a genetic test reporting species A.

We now have a new observation: the genetic test reports species A.

The test has:

$$
P(+\mid A)=0.8
$$

$$
P(+\mid B)=1-0.65=0.35
$$

Note that the second probability is the false-positive rate: a species B panda has a 35% chance of being identified as species A.

#### Part 1

Using equal prior probabilities:

$$
P(A\mid +)=
\frac{P(+\mid A)P(A)}
{P(+\mid A)P(A)+P(+\mid B)P(B)}
$$

$$
=\frac{(0.8)(0.5)}
{(0.8)(0.5)+(0.35)(0.5)}
$$

$$
=\frac{0.4}{0.575}
$$

$$
P(A\mid +)=\frac{16}{23}\approx69.57\%
$$

The positive genetic test favors species A, but because the test is imperfect, we do not have an extreme-valued probability.

#### Part 2

We already calculated\:

$$
P(A\mid T_1,S_2)=0.36
$$

$$
P(B\mid T_1,S_2)=0.64
$$

We can use these as our new priors when incorporating the test:

$$
P(A\mid T_1,S_2,+)
=\frac{P(+\mid A)P(A\mid T_1,S_2)}
{P(+\mid A)P(A\mid T_1,S_2)+P(+\mid B)P(B\mid T_1,S_2)}
$$

Substituting:

$$
=\frac{(0.8)(0.36)}
{(0.8)(0.36)+(0.35)(0.64)}
$$

$$
=\frac{0.288}{0.288+0.224}
$$

$$
P(A\mid T_1,S_2,+)=0.5625
$$



</details>
